title: Hyperkalaemia
clinicalScenario: Outline only. Planned scope: ECG-guided severity, membrane stabilisation, shifting agents (salbutamol, insulin with dextrose), removal, cause, monitoring, dialysis referral. Candidate sources to verify: UK Kidney Association treatment of acute hyperkalaemia in adults; Resuscitation Council UK; AHA ACLS special circumstances.

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult (over 18 years) Emergency Department (ED) recognition and treatment of acute hyperkalaemia, including hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest, based on the UK Kidney Association (UKKA) 2023 guideline and the 2025 European Resuscitation Council (ERC) special circumstances guideline. No Saudi national hyperkalaemia guideline was found; this protocol adopts the UKKA and ERC recommendations as the Saudi reference.
findings: Full protocol rebuilt from the source dossier opened on 2026-10-21; exact source locations are recorded in each investigation and medicine row.
The original outline remains preserved; this additive version is non-current and pending clinical review.
unverifiedSections: Normal reference ranges are typical adult values, not taken from the cited guidelines; ranges differ between laboratories.
Symptoms, examination signs, differentials, precipitants and the pathophysiology bullets are standard clinical content and were not extracted line by line from the opened sources.

No Saudi national or Saudi Ministry of Health hyperkalaemia guideline was found; the Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) status and availability of sodium zirconium cyclosilicate and patiromer were not checked.

The UKKA repeat-dose criteria for calcium, the patiromer frequency and cautions, and step 5 of the five-step approach were not found in the opened text; the choice of patiromer over sodium zirconium cyclosilicate is not stated as a condition.
Page and recommendation locators were taken from an automated reading of the guideline; check them against the PDF before clinical sign-off.
The pathway marks calcium gluconate as preferred outside resuscitation (UKKA Rec. 16.2b); the ERC 2025 text prefers calcium chloride for severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes.

UKKA 2023 hospital sections (pp. 58 onwards) were not available in the opened text, so preparation, dilution, repeat calcium dosing and renal-failure insulin dose reduction come from the Gloucestershire flowchart (past its March 2026 review date) and the 2020 Renal Association algorithm (past its stated review date). UKKA 2023 says calcium gluconate over 10 minutes while the 2020 algorithm and Gloucestershire say over 5 minutes; both are shown.

No insulin dose reduction for renal failure was found in the opened text; the Gloucestershire sheet's wording on glucose 20 mmol/L or higher was ambiguous and is not used. This protocol therefore applies the stated insulin dose at every eGFR and relies on the mandatory hourly glucose checks for 6 hours.
The calcium chloride and gluconate repeat limit, the bicarbonate dose and the patiromer duration were not stated in the opened text.

Renal, hepatic and age adjustments for the drugs added in this revision are from manufacturer labels (UK Summary of Product Characteristics, US prescribing information and a New Zealand data sheet), not from Saudi Food and Drug Authority labels.

pathophysiology.summary: Hyperkalaemia is a serum potassium of 5.5 mmol/L or above. It is dangerous because high extracellular potassium disturbs the electrical activity of the heart.
keyMechanisms: Potassium excretion falls in Acute Kidney Injury (AKI), chronic kidney disease and with drugs that block the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.
Potassium moves out of cells in acidosis, insulin deficiency, tissue breakdown (rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, crush injury) and with some drugs.
A high extracellular potassium raises the resting membrane potential and slows conduction, which produces peaked T waves, flattened P waves, a wide QRS complex and arrhythmias.
Treatment has three aims: protect the heart, shift potassium into cells, and remove potassium from the body.

symptoms: Often none; found on routine or acute blood tests.
physicalSigns: Reduced muscle power in severe cases.
redFlags: Potassium 6.0–6.4 mmol/L in a patient who is unwell or whose potassium is rising rapidly.
Oliguria or AKI with rising potassium.
precipitants: Medicines: renin–angiotensin system blockers, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim, potassium supplements and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
Tissue breakdown: rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis and burns.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Haemolysed or delayed sample with a normal ECG; repeat the test
Raised creatinine with low urine output
Very high creatine kinase, or known chemotherapy for tumour lysis

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate
actions: Get a 12-lead ECG for every hospital patient with potassium 6.0 mmol/L or above and start cardiac monitoring when indicated.
Use the five-step approach and never walk away without completing every step.
Step 1, protect the heart: for ECG changes give intravenous calcium (see Medicines); give it even if dialysis is immediately available.
Step 2, shift potassium into cells: insulin with glucose, with nebulised salbutamol as an adjunct (never alone).
Step 3, remove potassium: give sodium zirconium cyclosilicate for severe hyperkalaemia; calcium resonium is no longer routinely recommended.
Check blood glucose before and after insulin; give 10% glucose at 50 mL/hour for 5 hours if the pre-treatment glucose is below 7.0 mmol/L.
Do not use intravenous sodium bicarbonate for routine acute treatment.

clinicalManagement.title: Ongoing
actions: Monitor glucose at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, 300 and 360 minutes after insulin.
Repeat potassium at least 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 hours after moderate or severe hyperkalaemia is treated, and watch for rebound.
Find and treat the cause (AKI, medicines, tissue breakdown, acidosis) and stop medicines that raise potassium.

clinicalManagement.title: Escalation
actions: Potassium 6.5 mmol/L or above, or toxic ECG changes: urgent dialysis is recommended; give calcium without waiting.
Dialysis not immediately available: continue standard medical therapy.
Cardiac arrest: follow the Advanced Life Support (ALS) pathway and give calcium chloride and sodium bicarbonate (see the cardiac arrest branch).

clinicalManagement.title: Disposition
actions: Admit moderate or severe hyperkalaemia for monitoring and repeat potassium; severe hyperkalaemia needs immediate admission.
Mild hyperkalaemia in a well patient: repeat the test within 3 days, and within 1 day for moderate.

dischargeCriteria: Potassium back in the normal range on repeat testing, a normal ECG and the cause found and addressed.
Medicines that raise potassium reviewed before discharge.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Repeat potassium within 3 days for mild, within 1 day for moderate; severe hyperkalaemia needs immediate admission. Kidney or medicine review for recurrent hyperkalaemia, including whether a long-term potassium binder is needed.
